ideas.title: Budget-first company card
ideas.summary: When the company card is swiped, the purchase goes to the budgeting app first. The app approves or declines it against the budget, then the bank pays.

verdicts.note: Card platforms are built for this. Stripe Issuing sends each purchase to our app, which answers yes or no within 2 seconds (Lithic allows 6). The card has to be ours, not their old bank's card.
No new bank needed. The card platform's sponsor bank holds the money and the license; we make the yes or no call.
Ramp, Brex and Divvy sell credit cards. A debit card that stops at the budget line is open ground.
Money comes from a share of card fees plus a monthly plan. Get Stripe's and Lithic's real prices before promising anything.

ideas.next: Try it on DarkDorms first: one company card with one budget rule.

ideas.title: Limits on the whole bank account
ideas.summary: Set limits on one bank account so transfers and bills, not just card swipes, must fit the budget.

verdicts.note: Card swipes are easy to stop. Transfers and checks can only be stopped if the money sits in an account our partner runs, not at Chase or another outside bank.
Holding the business's main account brings more bank rules. Start with card spending, add accounts later.
Relay shows owners like a separate account per purpose. Hard limits on those would set us apart.

ideas.title: Start our own bank?
ideas.summary: Would the app need its own bank to sit between the card and the banking system?

verdicts.note: No. A charter takes 2 to 4 years and $2M to $5M+ (vendor estimate). A sponsor bank gives us the same card rails in weeks.
That money would mean investors or loans. A sponsor bank lets us start debt-free.

ideas.next: Revisit only if the app grows big enough that partner fees hurt.

ideas.title: Envelopes that refill from sales
ideas.summary: Every deposit splits into envelopes (taxes, inventory, payroll, owner pay). The card can only spend what is in the matching envelope.

verdicts.note: Relay sells up to 20 accounts to Profit First fans. Pairing envelopes with declines at the swipe is new.
Makes the tax set-aside automatic, like Penny's 25% rule for DarkDorms.
Envelopes are balances in our app; the yes or no check just reads them.

ideas.next: Make envelopes the heart of the first version.

ideas.title: Over budget? Text the owner
ideas.summary: When a worker's purchase is over budget, the owner gets a text and can say yes or no.

verdicts.note: The card network waits only about 2 seconds, too short for a text. So: decline, text the owner, and a Yes raises the limit so the worker can retry.
Small teams want this. It works like the Yes and No buttons on this island.

ideas.next: Design the decline, text, retry loop.

ideas.title: Built for debt-free owners
ideas.summary: Sell to owners who run their business debt-free (EntreLeadership and Profit First crowds), churches and nonprofits.

verdicts.note: These owners already avoid credit cards, and the big players all push credit.
It's a niche. Test demand with a simple waitlist page before building.

ideas.next: Draft a one-page waitlist site when you're ready.

ideas.title: Tech stack: Next.js web app on Vercel + Postgres
ideas.summary: Build the first version as a web app (Next.js, React, TypeScript) on Vercel, where DarkDorms already runs, with a Postgres database. Phone app later from the same code style.

verdicts.note: One language (TypeScript) front to back, free tiers to start, and Vercel is already set up.
Easy to test and deploy automatically on every change.

ideas.next: If yes: Quinn sets up an empty project in a new private GitHub repo you create.

ideas.title: Double-entry ledger with envelopes at the core
ideas.summary: Every dollar in the app lives in an envelope (taxes, inventory, payroll, owner pay). Every move is a balanced entry that can't be edited, only reversed, so the books always add up.

verdicts.note: This is how banks and card companies keep money correct. Building it first saves a rewrite later.
It's the heart of the debt-free promise: the card can only spend what an envelope holds.

ideas.next: If yes: Nova builds the ledger and envelopes with tests, no card yet.

ideas.title: Card prototype in Stripe Issuing test mode
ideas.summary: A free sandbox demo: a test card swipe asks our app, which checks the envelope and approves or declines within 2 seconds. No real cards, money or sign-ups.

verdicts.note: Stripe's test mode lets us build the real-time approve or decline with fake cards.
Fine in test mode. Going live needs Stripe's Issuing approval and a security review first.
This proves the budget-first card works before anyone applies for anything.

ideas.next: If yes: Pax builds the test-mode demo. Applying for live Issuing stays your call.
ideas.progress: Built in code; Stripe test mode waits for your OK

ideas.title: Link a business's bank to see balances
ideas.summary: Owners connect their bank so the app sees what's really there and can fill envelopes from it. Start read-only with Stripe Financial Connections; compare with Plaid.

verdicts.note: Read-only linking is the easy, low-risk first step.
We must store only tokens, never bank logins. Plan that before building.
Read-only access has far fewer rules than moving money.

ideas.next: If yes: Pax builds read-only bank linking in sandbox.

ideas.title: Ask-before-you-buy requests
ideas.summary: An employee who needs more than the envelope holds taps 'request $X for Y'. The owner gets a notice and taps yes or no. Yes moves money into the envelope, then the card works.

verdicts.note: Two taps for the employee, one for the owner.
The card only has 2 seconds at checkout, too short to ask a person. Asking before the purchase fixes that.
Owners of small teams want control without being the bottleneck.

ideas.next: If yes: Finn and Nova build it after the ledger.

ideas.title: Snap a receipt, auto-sort the spending
ideas.summary: After a purchase, the employee snaps the receipt. AI reads it, tags the category and attaches it to the transaction, ready for taxes.

verdicts.note: Useful and popular, but it needs an AI service with a cost per receipt. Later, after the core works.
Price the AI cost per receipt before promising it.

ideas.next: If yes: Quinn adds a data and AI specialist when the core is done.

ideas.title: Client intake form that writes the profile file
ideas.summary: A simple form a new client fills in (bio, achievements, strengths, photo, links). It drafts their content/profile.ts so Paige can build the site from it in minutes.

verdicts.note: The template already runs from one profile file. A form that fills it saves hours per client.
I can write the questions so the answers come back as great stories, not one-liners.
Clients find a form easier than a long chat.

ideas.next: If yes: Remy and Lyra write the questions, Paige wires the form into the template.

ideas.title: Theme gallery to show new clients
ideas.summary: One demo page where a client clicks through every theme (Neon, Executive and new ones) filled with sample content, then picks the one they want.

verdicts.note: Seeing it beats describing it. I'd add 2 new themes over time.
Uses demo content only, so no private details are shown.

ideas.next: If yes: Iris and Paige build the gallery with sample content.

ideas.title: Three fixed packages with clear prices
ideas.summary: Offer three packages (for example Starter, Pro, Premium) that say exactly what's included and how many revisions. You set the prices.

verdicts.note: Clear packages make yes easier and stop scope creep.
Prices are your call. We'll draft what's in each package and leave the prices blank.

ideas.next: If yes: Remy drafts the package contents for you to price.

ideas.title: Launch checklist: 90+ scores before any site goes live
ideas.summary: Every site must pass Dash's checklist before launch: Lighthouse 90+ on speed, accessibility and SEO, share preview set, no broken links, spelling checked.

verdicts.note: Free to run, and it catches the mistakes clients notice first.
Makes every site feel premium, every time.

ideas.next: If yes: Dash writes the checklist and runs it on your own portfolio first.

ideas.title: Monthly care plan for clients
ideas.summary: After launch, clients can stay on a monthly plan: small edits, new achievements added, photos swapped, and the site kept fast and up to date.

verdicts.note: Steady monthly income and happy repeat clients.
Only once we have a few clients. Price is your call.

ideas.next: If yes: Remy drafts what the plan includes; it starts after the first few clients.

ideas.title: Own-domain setup guide for clients
ideas.summary: A short step-by-step guide so each client can point their own domain (like janedoe.com) at their site, with Dash checking it works.

verdicts.note: Most clients want their own name as the address.
We never buy domains for clients; they buy them, we connect them.

ideas.next: If yes: Dash writes the guide.
